title: Enzymes, Photosynthesis and Cellular Respiration
seo_title: Year 11 Biology: Enzymes Photosynthesis and Respiration Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_code: Biology Unit 2: Cells as the basis of life
standard_text: Enzymes as biological catalysts and the factors that affect their activity; photosynthesis (light-dependent reactions and the Calvin cycle); aerobic and anaerobic respiration; ATP as the energy currency of cells; limiting factors. (Senior Secondary Biology, Unit 2: Cells and multicellular organisms)
meta_desc: Free Year 11 Biology worksheets on enzymes, photosynthesis and respiration: active sites, denaturation, inhibitors, light reactions, the Calvin cycle, glycolysis, ATP and limiting factors. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Photosynthesis stores energy; respiration releases it as ATP.
key_sub: Enzymes are proteins: too hot and the active site changes shape.
body_html:
How to think about it

Enzymes speed up reactions; the substrate fits the active site. Rate rises with temperature up to an optimum, then the enzyme is denatured. pH, substrate concentration and inhibitors also matter.

Photosynthesis: light-dependent reactions on the thylakoids make ATP and NADPH; the Calvin cycle in the stroma fixes CO₂ into sugars. Aerobic respiration: glycolysis (cytoplasm), Krebs cycle and electron transport chain (mitochondria) give about 30–38 ATP per glucose; anaerobic respiration gives 2.

Example

Rate 20 units at 25 °C, 30 units at 35 °C. Percentage increase?

(30 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100

Answer: 50%

Example

Pigment moves 3.0 cm; solvent 8.0 cm. Rf?

3.0 ÷ 8.0

Answer: 0.375

Common mistakes

  • Saying enzymes are ‘killed’ by heat: they are denatured (they were never alive).
  • Thinking plants do not respire: they respire all the time.
  • Placing glycolysis in the mitochondria: it happens in the cytoplasm.

faq.q: Why is photosynthesis called the reverse of respiration?
faq.a: Photosynthesis uses CO₂ and water to make glucose and oxygen, storing energy; respiration uses glucose and oxygen to make CO₂ and water, releasing energy as ATP.
The factor in shortest supply, which controls the rate: for photosynthesis it may be light, CO₂ or temperature.

items.q: What is made in anaerobic respiration in human muscle?
items.e: Yeast makes ethanol and CO₂ instead.

items.q: A starch solution takes 160 s to be broken down by amylase. Calculate the rate as 1/time.
Which class of enzymes is responsible for removing groups without hydrolysis, leaving double bonds?
items.e: Lyases: removing groups without hydrolysis, leaving double bonds.

items.q: How can you measure the rate of catalase activity?
c: measure the volume of oxygen released per minute
items.e: Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide.

items.q: What do lyases do?
c: removing groups without hydrolysis, leaving double bonds
transferring a group from one substrate to another
items.e: Lyases: removing groups without hydrolysis, leaving double bonds.

items.q: Why does the rate of an enzyme reaction rise between 10 °C and 35 °C?
c: molecules have more kinetic energy, so enzyme–substrate collisions are more frequent
items.e: Above the optimum, denaturation takes over.

items.q: What is NAD and NADP an example of?
items.e: NAD and NADP: coenzymes.

items.q: Which is an example of a competitive inhibitor in medicine?
c: a drug with a similar shape to the substrate
items.e: It competes for the active site.

items.q: At 25 °C the initial rate of an enzyme reaction is 20 units and at 35 °C it is 35 units. Calculate the percentage increase in rate.
What is the word equation for photosynthesis?
c: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (in light, with chlorophyll)
items.e: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.

items.q: At 25 °C the initial rate of an enzyme reaction is 36 units and at 35 °C it is 48 units. Calculate the percentage increase in rate.
Where does the Calvin cycle (light-independent reactions) take place?
c: in the stroma of the chloroplast
items.e: CO₂ is fixed by the enzyme RuBisCO.

items.q: Catalase releases 30 mL of oxygen in the first 120 s. Calculate the mean rate in mL per minute.
What is an enzyme–substrate complex?
c: the substrate bound to the enzyme's active site
an enzyme bound to an inhibitor
items.e: Products are released after the reaction.

items.q: What do ligases do?
c: joining two compounds together, such as C–O or C–N bonds
transferring a group from one substrate to another
items.e: Ligases: joining two compounds together, such as C–O or C–N bonds.

items.q: At 25 °C the initial rate of an enzyme reaction is 18 units and at 35 °C it is 45 units. Calculate the percentage increase in rate.
What is haem in haemoglobin an example of?
items.e: Haem in haemoglobin: a prosthetic group.

items.q: About how many ATP are made from one glucose in aerobic respiration?
items.e: Anaerobic respiration gives only 2.

items.q: Why does a high temperature stop an enzyme working?
c: hydrogen and ionic bonds break and the active site changes shape (denatures)
items.e: The substrate no longer fits.

items.q: At 25 °C the initial rate of an enzyme reaction is 40 units and at 35 °C it is 64 units. Calculate the percentage increase in rate.
Where do the light reactions of photosynthesis take place?
items.e: The dark reactions are in the stroma.

items.q: What is the role of NADP in photosynthesis?
c: it accepts electrons and protons, becoming reduced NADP
items.e: Reduced NADP is used to reduce GP.

items.q: Why does the rate of photosynthesis fall at very high temperatures?
c: enzymes such as rubisco are denatured
items.e: Stomata may also close.

items.q: What does chlorophyll absorb mainly?
items.e: Green light is reflected.

items.q: Where does glycolysis take place?
items.e: Glucose is split into two pyruvate.

items.q: How is ATP made in the light-dependent reaction?
c: protons flow through ATP synthase down a gradient (chemiosmosis)
items.e: This is photophosphorylation.

items.q: Where does the Calvin cycle (light-independent reaction) take place?
items.e: It uses ATP and reduced NADP.

items.q: In a chromatogram of leaf pigments, a pigment spot moves 5.4 cm and the solvent moves 8.0 cm. Calculate its R<sub>f</sub> value.
In a chromatogram of leaf pigments, a pigment spot moves 5.4 cm and the solvent moves 12 cm. Calculate its R<sub>f</sub> value.
What is the word equation for aerobic respiration?
c: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ ATP)
items.e: It releases energy as ATP.

items.q: Which photosystem is used in cyclic photophosphorylation?
c: both PS I and PS II
items.e: It makes ATP but no NADPH or O₂.

items.q: What is Calvin cycle?
c: large bundle-sheath cells around the veins of C₄ leaves
the cycle in the stroma that fixes CO₂ into sugar
a reaction centre chlorophyll an absorbing best at 680 nm (P680)
the enzyme that fixes CO₂ onto RuBP
items.e: Calvin cycle: the cycle in the stroma that fixes CO₂ into sugar.

items.q: What is photorespiration?
c: large bundle-sheath cells around the veins of C₄ leaves
the splitting of water that releases oxygen
RuBisCO binding O₂ instead of CO₂, wasting energy
a reaction centre chlorophyll an absorbing best at 700 nm (P700)
items.e: Photorespiration: RuBisCO binding O₂ instead of CO₂, wasting energy.

items.q: Where do the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis take place?
c: on the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast
items.e: Chlorophyll is in the thylakoids.

items.q: What do the light-dependent reactions supply to the Calvin cycle?
items.e: Water is split and oxygen is released.

items.q: What is a limiting factor?
c: a factor that stops a reaction for ever
the factor that is in shortest supply and so controls the rate
the factor that is present in excess
the temperature at which an enzyme denatures
items.e: Light, CO₂ and temperature limit photosynthesis.

items.q: Where does the Calvin cycle take place?
c: in the stroma of the chloroplast
items.e: It uses ATP and NADPH.

items.q: Why do growers burn paraffin in greenhouses?
c: it raises CO₂ concentration and temperature
items.e: Both can limit photosynthesis.

items.q: What is the name for RuBisCO binding O₂ instead of CO₂, wasting energy?
items.e: Photorespiration: RuBisCO binding O₂ instead of CO₂, wasting energy.

items.q: What is an enzyme?
c: a lipid in the cell membrane
a protein that is a biological catalyst
items.e: Enzymes speed up reactions and are not used up.

items.q: What is the net gain of ATP when 2 molecules of glucose are broken down by glycolysis alone?
items.e: Net 2 ATP per glucose (4 made, 2 used): 4 ATP.

items.q: How many molecules of pyruvic acid are formed from 10 molecules of glucose in glycolysis?
items.e: Each glucose gives 2 pyruvic acid: 2 × 10 = 20.

items.q: Why is respiration called an amphibolic pathway?
c: it happens in water and on land
it is used both for breaking down and for building molecules
items.e: Intermediates are used to make fats and proteins.

items.q: A competitive inhibitor slows an enzyme. How does it work?
c: it has a similar shape to the substrate and blocks the active site
items.e: Adding more substrate reduces its effect.

items.q: What are cristae?
c: folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane
items.e: They give a large surface area for the electron transfer chain.

items.q: What is produced in anaerobic respiration in yeast?
items.e: This is alcoholic fermentation.

items.q: Which molecule can be respired if glucose runs out?
items.e: Fatty acids enter as acetyl CoA.

items.q: What is the first product of the Krebs cycle?
items.e: Acetyl CoA + oxaloacetic acid → citric acid.

items.q: What is the net gain of ATP when 1 molecule of glucose are broken down by glycolysis alone?
items.e: Net 2 ATP per glucose (4 made, 2 used): 2 ATP.

items.q: Why does each enzyme work on only one substrate?
c: the active site has a shape that fits only that substrate
all substrates have the same shape
enzymes are too large for other substrates
enzymes are used up after one reaction
items.e: Lock-and-key and induced-fit models.

items.q: Why is a respirometer kept at constant temperature?
c: temperature changes gas volume and enzyme activity
items.e: Use a water bath and a control tube.

items.q: Why does anaerobic respiration make much less ATP?
c: only glycolysis produces ATP; the Krebs cycle and electron transfer chain stop
items.e: Only 2 ATP per glucose.

items.q: An organism takes in 40 mL of oxygen and gives out 36 mL of carbon dioxide. Calculate the respiratory quotient.
items.e: RQ = CO₂ given out ÷ O₂ taken in = 0.900 (1.0 for carbohydrate, about 0.7 for lipid, about 0.9 for protein).

items.q: What is the respiratory quotient (RQ) of carbohydrates?
items.e: CO₂ given out = O₂ taken in.

items.q: What is the net gain of ATP when 5 molecules of glucose are broken down by glycolysis alone?
items.e: Net 2 ATP per glucose (4 made, 2 used): 10 ATP.

items.q: What is the final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration?
items.e: Oxygen combines with electrons and protons to form water.

items.q: Which factor would NOT increase the rate of photosynthesis in a plant already in bright light at 25 °C with low CO₂?
c: a slightly warmer temperature up to the optimum
items.e: When CO₂ is limiting, extra light makes no difference.

items.q: Which is used in respiration if carbohydrates run out?
items.e: Fats enter as acetyl CoA, proteins as amino acids.

items.q: What is the role of ATP in cells?
c: it carries energy from respiration to reactions that need it
it is the main component of membranes
items.e: ATP → ADP + Pi releases energy.

items.q: What is produced in anaerobic respiration in mammals?
items.e: Pyruvate is reduced, regenerating NAD.

items.q: Where does the oxygen given out in photosynthesis come from?
items.e: Shown with heavy-oxygen isotopes.

items.q: What is Kranz anatomy?
c: the cycle in the stroma that fixes CO₂ into sugar
RuBisCO binding O₂ instead of CO₂, wasting energy
the splitting of water that releases oxygen
large bundle-sheath cells around the veins of C₄ leaves
items.e: Kranz anatomy: large bundle-sheath cells around the veins of C₄ leaves.

items.q: What is the Z scheme?
c: the zig-zag path of electrons from PS II to PS I in non-cyclic photophosphorylation
items.e: Electrons go up in energy twice.

items.q: Why is anaerobic respiration much less efficient than aerobic respiration?
c: it makes no ATP at all
glucose is only partly broken down, so much less ATP is made
items.e: Energy is left in lactate or ethanol.

items.q: What is the law of limiting factors?
c: the rate is limited by the factor that is nearest its minimum value
the largest factor controls the rate
items.e: Proposed by Blackman.

items.q: What happens in human muscles during heavy exercise when oxygen is short?
c: pyruvic acid is reduced to lactic acid
items.e: This causes fatigue.

items.q: What is the primary CO₂ acceptor in C₄ plants?
items.e: PEP carboxylase fixes CO₂ in mesophyll cells.

items.q: Where in the cell does the electron transport chain take place?
items.e: The electron transport chain: the inner mitochondrial membrane.

items.q: Where in the cell does the Krebs cycle take place?
items.e: The Krebs cycle: the mitochondrial matrix.

items.q: Which wavelengths of light are absorbed most by chlorophyll a?
items.e: Green is reflected.

items.q: What is formed when pyruvate enters the mitochondrion?
c: acetyl CoA, with release of CO₂ and NADH
items.e: This is oxidative decarboxylation.

items.q: What is the net gain of ATP from glycolysis of one glucose?
items.e: 4 are made but 2 are used.

items.q: What is the name for a reaction centre chlorophyll an absorbing best at 700 nm (P700)?
items.e: PS I: a reaction centre chlorophyll an absorbing best at 700 nm (P700).

items.q: How many molecules of pyruvic acid are formed from 2 molecules of glucose in glycolysis?
items.e: Each glucose gives 2 pyruvic acid: 2 × 2 = 4.

items.q: Where does the electron transport chain of aerobic respiration take place?
c: on the inner membrane (cristae) of the mitochondrion
items.e: Most ATP is made here.

items.q: What is the RQ of fats such as tripalmitin?
items.e: Fats need more oxygen to burn.

items.q: Which organism makes ethanol and CO₂ by fermentation?
items.e: Used in making bread and alcohol.

items.q: What is the name for the enzyme that fixes CO₂ onto RuBP?
items.e: RuBisCO: the enzyme that fixes CO₂ onto RuBP.

items.q: What is the net gain of ATP when 4 molecules of glucose are broken down by glycolysis alone?
items.e: Net 2 ATP per glucose (4 made, 2 used): 8 ATP.

items.q: What is the net gain of ATP when 9 molecules of glucose are broken down by glycolysis alone?
items.e: Net 2 ATP per glucose (4 made, 2 used): 18 ATP.

items.q: In a chromatogram of leaf pigments, a pigment spot moves 2.0 cm and the solvent moves 8.0 cm. Calculate its R<sub>f</sub> value.
Why does the rate of an enzyme reaction level off at high substrate concentration?
c: all the active sites are occupied
items.e: Enzyme concentration is now the limiting factor.

items.q: In a chromatogram of leaf pigments, a pigment spot moves 5.4 cm and the solvent moves 9.0 cm. Calculate its R<sub>f</sub> value.
A starch solution takes 50 s to be broken down by amylase. Calculate the rate as 1/time.
Where do the light-dependent reactions take place?
items.e: Chlorophyll is in photosystems in the thylakoids.

items.q: Where is lipase produced?
items.e: It breaks lipids into fatty acids and monoglycerides.

items.q: Why are enzymes specific?
c: only one substrate has a complementary shape to the active site
items.e: The tertiary structure decides the shape.

items.q: What is RuBP?
c: a 5-carbon compound that combines with CO₂ in the Calvin cycle
items.e: Ribulose bisphosphate is regenerated using ATP.

items.q: In a chromatogram of leaf pigments, a pigment spot moves 3.0 cm and the solvent moves 8.0 cm. Calculate its R<sub>f</sub> value.
What is photolysis?
c: light splitting water into protons, electrons and oxygen
items.e: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂.

items.q: A starch solution takes 125 s to be broken down by amylase. Calculate the rate as 1/time.
In a chromatogram of leaf pigments, a pigment spot moves 4.2 cm and the solvent moves 12 cm. Calculate its R<sub>f</sub> value.
A starch solution takes 32 s to be broken down by amylase. Calculate the rate as 1/time.
How does a non-competitive inhibitor work?
c: it binds to the active site
it binds away from the active site and changes its shape
it raises the activation energy only
items.e: More substrate does not reduce its effect.

items.q: Why does increasing temperature (below the optimum) speed up an enzyme reaction?
c: molecules have more kinetic energy, so there are more successful collisions
items.e: More enzyme–substrate complexes form.

items.q: In a chromatogram of leaf pigments, a pigment spot moves 1.5 cm and the solvent moves 8.0 cm. Calculate its R<sub>f</sub> value.
What is the effect of a cofactor such as chloride ions on amylase?
c: it helps the enzyme work or bind its substrate
items.e: Many enzymes need cofactors.

items.q: In a chromatogram of leaf pigments, a pigment spot moves 4.2 cm and the solvent moves 9.0 cm. Calculate its R<sub>f</sub> value.
Which enzyme fixes carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle?
items.e: CO₂ + RuBP → 2 GP.

items.q: At 25 °C the initial rate of an enzyme reaction is 30 units and at 35 °C it is 42 units. Calculate the percentage increase in rate.
